newsitem.title: USA: MCI shares plunge on worries over earnings, merger.
newsitem.headline: MCI shares plunge on worries over earnings, merger.

text.p: MCI Communications Corp. stock tumbled Friday after it said losses from entering local phone markets would hurt earnings, sparking concern about its planned $24 billion merger with British Telecommunications Plc.

MCI stock lost $7.375 to $35 and was the most active issue on Nasdaq. The nation's No. 2 long-distance company said late Thursday that losses from investments in local service could exceed $800 million, double its prior estimates, hurting earnings for the rest of 1997 and all of 1998.
British Telecom said Friday that it could not rule out renegotiating its planned merger with MCI, but a spokesman said it was too soon to draw any conclusions about the deal.
"At this stage, we are simply looking at the figures, and anything beyond that is premature," he said.
British Telecom's stock also tumbled, falling in London and New York.
MCI, based in Washington, said Friday that BT had been kept fully informed about MCI's investments in local service and that it expected the merger to go ahead.
"MCI's view is that the merger is going forward as planned," spokesman Jim Monroe said. "We are still hopeful that the we are going to close the merger by the fall."

British Telecom "has been in alliance with us for four years, they hold board positions and they have a clear view of the announcements we made yesterday," Monroe said. BT's chief executive, Sir Peter Bonfield, sits on MCI's board.
Takeover experts on Wall Street said BT may cut the price it is willing to pay for MCI, which earned $1.2 billion, or $1.73 a share, on sales of $18.5 billion last year.

"Number one, the deal gets done," said one takeover expert. "All the strategic rationale is still there, but it clearly warrants a price cut. The questions are: how big are the problems and is it a one-time shot or ongoing?"

The deal, first announced in November, calls for BT to exchange 0.54 of its American Depositary Receipts and $6 in cash for each MCI share in a deal valued at about $24 billion at the time. After the merger, MCI shareholders would own 34 percent of the new company, to be called Concert Plc.
When the deal was announced, BT and MCI said Concert would have annual revenues of more than $42 billion and 43 million business and residential customers in 70 countries.
But some analysts said they thought it unlikely BT would seek to renegotiate a deal it has championed as a strategic coup since announcing it in November.
"I think any renegotiation would be a loss of face and more importantly damage confidence in BT's ability to deliver strategic goals," said Andrew Harrington at Salomon Bros. in London.

Jack Grubman at Salomon Bros. in New York also dismissed speculation the merger was at risk. "One could argue the industrial logic behind the BT-MCI merger was to allow MCI to do what they are doing, namely more aggressively attack Bell local markets," he wrote in a research note Friday.
Analysts also said MCI's comments were designed to pressure regulators to take action to speed the entry of new competitors into the local phone business.

MCI said it planned to push ahead to compete in U.S. local phone markets. It blamed the losses on delays by regional phone companies in opening up their markets to long-distance rivals, as is required under the sweeping overhaul of U.S. telecommunications law passed last year.
